overview: Chinook communities made the lower Columbia River and its Pacific coast a busy center of river life. Today the Chinook Indian Nation joins five constituent groups. The map’s 1492 to 1500 outline covers part of this region, not every Chinookan community or the full span of Chinook history.

sections.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar

items.text: The present Chinook Indian Nation identifies Lower Chinook, Clatsop, Kathlamet, Wahkiakum and Willapa as its constituent groups. Their communities lie around the river mouth and neighboring shores. This modern political association should not be mistaken for a single ancient empire governing every Chinookan-speaking village upriver.

Cedar plankhouses could shelter several related families, each with its own fire. In a 1902 account, Catherine George remembered houses at Gray’s Bay with several household fires. Seasonal movement could also involve lighter summer shelters. A village was therefore a community of households whose living arrangements changed with work and season.

Household society had inequalities. The community-reviewed history describes leading families toward the back of a plankhouse and commoners and enslaved people nearer the front. Large shared houses were places of kinship and cooperation, but also of unequal power and, for enslaved residents, a lack of freedom.

Cathlapotle, farther upriver near modern Ridgefield, offers a regional Chinookan comparison outside this map outline. Excavators recorded house depressions, hearths and post traces. These buried features preserve the layout of wooden buildings even when their walls have disappeared; they do not establish a coastal Chinook capital.

Cathlapotle’s fish remains include salmon, sturgeon and smelt, with smaller fish also represented. Some excavated deposits held dense concentrations of bones. Archaeologists can study discarded meals to learn about fishing and processing: yesterday’s kitchen rubbish becomes tomorrow’s research material.

Trade beads and pieces of Chinese porcelain at Cathlapotle connect a river town to the overseas fur-trade era. One porcelain fragment had been reshaped into a scraper. Imported objects were not simply stored as curiosities; someone could give a broken piece a new working life.

Canoes carried people and goods through networks linking the coast and the interior. Small gathering boats served short trips, while larger craft carried cargo and traveled coastal waters. A canoe could be everyday transport, a fishing platform and a connection to relatives in another settlement.

Carver Tony Johnson describes placing depth pegs in a canoe hull so that hollowing could stop at the intended thickness. Hot stones and water then produced steam to soften and spread the sides. A graceful wooden boat required careful measuring as well as strength and patience.

Cedar supplied much more than boat hulls. The project’s account describes bark made into water-resistant clothing, roots used for baskets and shredded material used for baby diapers. The same tree could help a family travel, carry supplies and look after its smallest members.

sections.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample

items.text: An epidemic in 1830 and 1831 killed many lower Columbia people, including the influential leader Comcomly. Survivors regrouped in communities along the river and Willapa Bay. The loss of relatives and neighbors altered settlement and family life; it did not erase Chinook people from their homeland.

At Tansy Point in 1851, Native leaders resisted removal east of the Cascades. Treaties negotiated there promised provisions and continuing residence in their homeland, but were never ratified. Chinook scholar Rachel Cushman connects this failure with family memories of a hungry winter when promised food did not arrive.

A modern Cathlapotle plankhouse opened in 2005 after more than a hundred volunteers worked on the reconstruction. Archaeology informed the building, which became a setting for education and tribal events. This is a new structure supporting living communities, not a surviving wooden house from the fifteenth century.

In 2019 the Chinook Indian Nation completed the purchase of ten acres at Tansy Point. Cushman describes the fundraising and community effort that made it possible. Recovering land at the treaty site created a place for commemoration and future restoration work, turning historical memory into a practical commitment.

Chinuk Wawa developed as a language of communication among different peoples, drawing on Chinookan languages and other sources. The nation recommends resources in it today. It must be distinguished from the older Chinookan languages and from the assumption that everyone in this coastal region spoke identically.

A short written sample is “kakwa nsayka ulman-tilixam laska munk-kemteks nsayka”, translated “As Our Elders Teach Us to Speak It”. This is the parallel title of Grand Ronde’s 2012 Chinuk Wawa dictionary, in the spelling recorded by Smithsonian’s catalogue. It is a modern teaching witness, not a sentence dated to 1492.

Federal acknowledgement granted in 2001 was reversed in 2002. The Bureau of Indian Affairs still describes the Chinook Indian Nation as non-federally recognized on its current historical-background page. That administrative status concerns the relationship with the United States; Chinook families and national cultural life continue.

ending.text: There was no Chinook ending in 1500. Despite epidemic loss, land dispossession and the continuing recognition struggle, the nation maintains stories, language and community traditions. The imported date marks the end of this map record only.
